content: The scalp is the anatomical region that is bordered anteriorly by the face and laterally and posteriorly by the neck. The scalp is typically described as having five distinct layers, which can be remembered using the mnemonic SCALP: S (Skin): The outermost layer of the scalp is the skin, from which hair grows. This layer is highly vascularized and prone to conditions such as dandruff and cutis verticis gyrata. C (Connective tissue): Beneath the skin lies a thin layer of fat and fibrous connective tissue. A (Aponeurosis): The aponeurosis, also known as the galea aponeurotica, is a tough, dense fibrous tissue layer. It extends from the frontalis muscle at the front of the head to the occipitalis muscle at the back. L (Loose areolar connective tissue): This layer provides a plane of separation between the upper three layers and the pericranium. It is the layer through which the scalp is torn during scalping injuries. It also serves as a surgical access plane in craniofacial and neurosurgical procedures. This layer is sometimes referred to as the Danger Zone because infections can easily spread through it to the emissary veins, which drain into the cranial cavity. The loose areolar tissue in this layer is composed of random collagen type I bundles, collagen type III, and is rich in glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). It is highly vascular and cellular, with more extracellular matrix than fibers. P (Pericranium): The pericranium is the periosteum of the skull bones. It provides nutrition to the bone and facilitates repair. During procedures such as craniotomy, the pericranium can be lifted from the bone to allow the removal of bone windows. The blood supply to the scalp is derived from four pairs of arteries, two from the external carotid artery and two from the internal carotid artery: Internal carotid artery branches: The supratrochlear artery supplies the midline of the forehead. The supraorbital artery supplies the lateral forehead and the scalp up to the vertex. External carotid artery branches: The superficial temporal artery provides frontal and parietal branches, supplying much of the scalp. The occipital artery supplies the posterior scalp. The innervation of the scalp is as follows: The supratrochlear nerve and supraorbital nerve, branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, innervate the anterior scalp. The greater occipital nerve (C2) provides sensation to the posterior scalp up to the vertex. The lesser occipital nerve (C3) innervates the area behind the ear. The zygomaticotemporal nerve, a branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, supplies the hairless temple region. The auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, innervates the lateral scalp. The scalp plays a significant role in facial aesthetics. Androgenic alopecia, or male pattern hair loss, is a common concern among men. Treatment options include medications such as finasteride or hair transplantation, with varying degrees of success. With aging, the scalp may become heavy and loose, leading to a low, heavy, and deeply lined forehead. These changes can be addressed through procedures such as a brow lift.
